Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you, that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light, by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ (1)

Thus the Truth, glory be to Him, opens this surah with the disjointed letters (alif) (lam) (ra). We have already said that these are tawqifi letters (letters whose meaning and use are fixed by revelation), which the Messenger of Allah conveyed to us as he heard them from Jibril, upon him be peace.

However, it is noticeable that these disjointed tawqifi letters did not come alone in this surah as a separate verse, like His saying at the beginning of Surah Qaf:

﴿Qaf.﴾ (Qaf)

This is a verse by itself. And as it came in other surahs with disjointed letters, it was recorded as verses. Here, however, the disjointed tawqifi letters come as part of the verse.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you...﴾ (Ibrahim)

The word (kitab) (Book), when used without qualification, refers its meaning to the Qur'an. It is called a Book (kitab), it is called a Qur'an (qur'an), it is called a revelation (tanzil), and it has many names.

The word (kitab) indicates that it is written, and the word (Qur'an) indicates that it is read (to be recited). These two names are the foundation among the names of the Qur'an, because it is a Book that is written and a Qur'an that is recited.

Thus the companion (2) who collected the Qur'an would not write down a verse unless he found it written and found it recited by two of the Companions. So the Qur'an is a Book whose writing is established with proof from the time of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is recited, as the word (Qur'an) indicates.

His saying, the Truth:

﴿We have sent it down to you...﴾ (Ibrahim)

indicates that it came from above.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says elsewhere about the Qur'an:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and a guidance, a mercy and good tidings for the Muslims.﴾ (An-Nahl 89)

He also says elsewhere:

﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended...﴾ (Al-Isra' 105)

Sometimes He attributes the descent to the One who brought it, and sometimes He attributes the descent to the Being whom the Truth sent with the Qur'an to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, namely Jibril, upon him be peace.

So His saying: ﴿We have sent it down...﴾ (Ibrahim) refers to the transfer from the realm of the Preserved Tablet so that it may take up its task in existence. The purpose of sending down the Qur'an to you, O Muhammad, is:

﴿that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light...﴾ (Ibrahim)

We notice here that the Qur'an was sent down for all people, and the Truth, glory be to Him, did not say to him what He said to the earlier messengers before the Messenger of Allah, for the mission of each of them was restricted to specific peoples, such as His saying:

﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud...﴾ (Al-A'raf 65)

And His saying, the Truth:

﴿And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb...﴾ (Al-A'raf 85)

And likewise His saying to Musa:

﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel...﴾ (Al 'Imran 49)

Thus every messenger was sent by Allah to a particular place, to particular people, and in a particular time, except Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, whom Allah sent to all mankind.

The example before us is when he, peace and blessings be upon him, judged with truth between a Muslim and a Jew, and ruled in favour of the Jew, because the truth was with him (3). The truth, in the sight of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was dearer to him than one who claims to be a Muslim.

Thus we see that His saying, the Truth:

﴿that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light...﴾ (Ibrahim)

is evidence of the universality of the message, and His saying reinforces it:

﴿Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all...﴾ (Al-A'raf 158)

By this, the argument of those who said he was sent only to the Arabs is refuted.

Here we find two distinctions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him.

The first distinction: that the Truth, glory be to Him, chose him as a messenger; mere selection for that task is a high rank.

The second distinction: that he is a messenger to all mankind, and this is another high rank, because it encompasses place and time, tongues and peoples.

Then comes the miraculous quality in His saying:

﴿that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light...﴾ (Ibrahim)

He did not say "out of the darknesses into the lights." He willed that darkness be mentioned in the plural and light in the singular, because light is one and does not multiply, whereas darknesses multiply according to the multiplicity of desires: one darkness here and another darkness there.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, brings us out of the many darknesses according to human desires, this is grace and blessing from Him, because we come out into the one light.

Thus Allah wills to clarify the meaning through sensory things that everyone perceives. There is no doubt that darkness conceals things, so that a person may collide with what he would otherwise avoid, and so he refrains from walking with confidence, for if he strikes something, he may break it or it may break him. Thus darkness prevents a person from finding what he seeks.

As for light, it makes things clear, and a person can distinguish between paths, avoid what harms him, and turn toward what benefits him, and be upon insight from guidance. That is the sensory matter, and both light and darkness are sensory matters.

Thus Allah clarifies meanings for us. Life does not need only that which makes material appearances clear by light; it also needs a light that makes spiritual appearances clear: of hatred and envy, fear and security, tranquillity, trustworthiness, loyalty, and other things.

Life as a whole contains a thing and its opposite, so meanings must also be made clear. The light that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, brought makes clear both the sensory and the meaningful at once, so that we avoid the things that darkness obscures, and walk with clear insight into meanings, and do not collide with obstacles.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, explains the spiritual matter to us, saying:

﴿to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ (Ibrahim)

This is the straight path to which Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, brings us out of darknesses into his light.

The Truth, glory be to Him, wants to make the way to this path clear to us, because it may be wearisome for some. So He wishes to combine for us two things: a clear, evident way by which a person reaches the goal with ease, and another way which is not clear, in which things are not manifest.

He brought in darkness and light to clarify this meaning for us: the straight path is the shortest means to the desired goal of life in this world and the Hereafter, and the path of darknesses is the unsafe path.

The Truth, glory be to Him, attributes the path to which the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, brings us out:

﴿to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ (Ibrahim)

The Almighty (al-'Aziz) is the One who overcomes and is not overcome. The Praiseworthy (al-Hamid) is the One for whom the attribute of praise has been established by others; and even if no praise has come from others, He is praiseworthy in His essence, and He must be praised, even though whether you praise Him or do not praise Him, He is praiseworthy.

To God belongs the highest likeness, and He is exalted above every equal or similar. In our worldly life we find someone of whom it is said that he is praiseworthy in his qualities, even if no one praises him, yet in everything that proceeds from him, care is taken that he be praiseworthy.

But among people, the one praised is a created being, whereas the praise belonging to the Truth is absolute. A essence is not praiseworthy or praised unless it possesses the attributes that make it worthy of the favour which a person must praise.

The sound nature in a human being receives this universe, which was prepared before it existed to receive it, and loves to praise the One who made this universe, even though a person's praising or not praising adds nothing to the One who prepared this universe and created it, for He is praiseworthy in His essence.

If you praise Him, this is for your own benefit, and in this there is guidance to the path of the Almighty, who is not overcome, and the Praiseworthy, who deserves praise, even if no one praises Him, because His attributes are eternal.

Allah is the Creator before He created creation; He is the Provider before the provided-for was created; He is the Honourer before anyone honours Him; He is praised before anyone praises Him; He is the Accepter of repentance before anyone repents to Him.

He, glory be to Him, acts by His attribute, whereas a person does not act unless he performs the attribute. You do not know that so-and-so is generous except because you see him giving with liberality and open-handedness, whereas Allah is the Generous before anyone is honoured by Him.

He said: "Give him his right." He said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, I cannot pay it; I have told him that you are sending us to Khaybar, and I hope you will give us some spoil, and I will return and pay him." He said: "Give him his right." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, when he said something three times, was not contradicted. Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 2:

He, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.﴾

If you recite this verse joined to what precedes it, you will recite it as:

﴿The path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy. Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ (Ibrahim)

And if you are going to recite it separated from what precedes it, you will say:

﴿Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.﴾ (Ibrahim)

You will pronounce the word (Allah) without tarqiq (thinning of the vowel), unlike when you recite it joined, where you must pronounce it with tarqiq.

The principles of the language require that a proper noun (ism 'alam) denoting the essence comes first, followed by the attribute. You say: "I met so-and-so the poet, or the writer, or the scholar." But here the matter has come in a different order:

﴿The path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ (Ibrahim)

That is, He put (the Almighty, the Praiseworthy) first, then came the word of majesty, (Allah), which is the proper name for the Necessarily Existent. This happened because the proper name indicates the named entity regardless of its attributes, and then the attributes come to it.

Among the scholars there are those who said that it is derived (mushtaq), meaning that (Allah) signifies the one truly worshipped, and the attribute of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy is a reason (haythiyya) for His being truly worshipped, glorified is He.

And among the scholars are those who said: the word (Allah) is a proper name, not a derived noun, and so it has absolute ownership.

﴿To Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth..﴾ (Ibrahim)

Nothing occurs in this dominion except what He wills. Whoever believes in Him does justice to his self, his life, and his hereafter. As for whoever does not believe in Him, he has the opposite, which is His saying, the Truth:

﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.﴾ (Ibrahim)

This woe is not only in the Hereafter but also in this world, because when a person is confronted with difficulties, obstacles, and calamities for which he has no means to repel them, the believer here can remember that he has a Lord above all means, and he finds rest in the aid of the Truth, glorified is He. Thus he feels that he has a store in this world on which he relies in facing great events.

As for the non-believer, he has nothing before him but despair; therefore we find the spread of suicide among non-believers, because there are events beyond their means which they cannot repel, and they have no faith in a Lord to whom they can return.

Therefore, when I read the exegetes who explain the word (al-Waył) as the punishment of the Hereafter, I find myself saying: rather, woe also occurs in this world, because many events of life occur beyond a person's means; if a person did not believe in God, he would be terrified from excess despair.

For this reason we find some people, when they find no escape, saying "O Lord," and in doing so they proclaim the cry of the primordial nature (fitra), which they resisted with atheism and disbelief, and this woe has an extension in a more intense form in the Hereafter.

1 Al-waył: a word meaning punishment, a supplication for evil, and a warning of it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/362] And al-waył: ruin, invoked upon one who falls into punishment or a destruction he deserves. [Lisan al-Arab, entry: w-y-l]

Al-Sha'rawi, on the words of Allah, describes those who do not believe. He says:

﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter, and bar (others) from the way of Allah, and seek to make it crooked. Those are in far-off error.﴾

Here we find the root ḥ-b-b (ḥ-b-b, "love"). Among its curiosities is that the verb may be quadriliteral: we say aḥabba fulān ("so-and-so loved"), and we say of the one who is loved, maḥbūb ("beloved"). This means there is a mutual connection between the two. In the case where there is no such connection, it is said ḥabba yuḥibbu, ḥābb and muḥibb.

The difference between aḥabba and istaḥabba is noticeable in the coming of the sīn and the tā', which are a sign of seeking (ṭalab). On this basis, istaḥabba means that the one who loves has not been content with the natural matter, but has forced love upon himself and gone to excess in it.

An example of this is found in everyday life. We see someone who drifts into some deviation, but he does not love to be a lover of this deviation at the same time; he commits the deviation while hating it, and he may strike himself and blame himself because it drifts him into this deviation.

And we find another who deviates because he loves this deviation and immerses himself in it, loves this immersion, speaks of this deviation, and loves within himself that he loved that disobedience, because it fulfils for him a immediate desire. This is the one who "prefers" (istaḥabba), because he has exceeded love beyond its natural limit.

When you examine the noble verse closely, you find that it does not forbid you from loving the world, but speaks of preferring it over the Hereafter; this is the blameworthy matter. As for if you love the world because it helps you with the obligations of your religion and you make it a field (mazraʿah) for the Hereafter, this is a required matter, because you do in it what makes you happy in your Hereafter. This is seeking the world for the sake of the Hereafter.

For this reason, consider His saying in Surat al-Muʾminun:

﴿And those who are active in giving zakat.﴾ (al-Muʾminun)

He does not merely pay zakat, but works in order to bring for himself and his dependants sustenance, and exerts effort so that he has a surplus from which zakat is paid. Therefore he does not work merely according to his need, but according to his capacity, so as to achieve what he can give to one who cannot work.

For this reason Allah the Exalted did not say: (والذين هم للزكاة مؤدّون, "those who are paying zakat"), but said:

﴿And those who are active in giving zakat.﴾ (al-Muʾminun)

Here we do not find those who prefer life in order to make it a field for the Hereafter; rather, they prefer life:

﴿And bar (others) from the way of Allah..﴾ (Ibrahim)

That is: they were not content with preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter alone, nor with walking the path of desires and pleasures and ruining themselves, but they went far in misguidance and barred others from the way of Allah.

And we find Allah the Exalted say in another place:

﴿Why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked..﴾ (Al 'Imran)

They had gone astray in themselves, and were not content with that, but tried to mislead others and bar them from guidance.

Then comes a new stage:

﴿And seek to make it crooked..﴾ (Ibrahim)

That is: they seek the law of Allah to be crooked so that their whims may be fulfilled. Thus we find three degrees of misguidance: preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter, barring from the way of Allah, and distorting the method so that people come to hate it.

Allah the Exalted describes these:

﴿Those are in far-off error.﴾ (Ibrahim)

That is: the people of the first degree of misguidance are those who preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter; those who went deeper into error are those who bar from the way of Allah; and those who went deeper and deeper are those who distort the method of Allah in order to repel people from it, or so that their whims may be fulfilled. Thus they travelled to the farthest region of error.

² Al-Ghayy: misguidance, perdition and corruption. [Lisan al-Arab, root: gh-w-y]. And ghawā means he failed and strayed, because he was immersed in ignorance. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/64].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 4:

Allah, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them. Then Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He is the Almighty, the Wise.﴾

We know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a conveyor of Allah's methodology (manhaj), and is supported by a miracle that establishes his truthfulness in what he conveyed to those to whom he was sent. Allah, glorified is He, had already related what happened to the nations before the nation of Muhammad ﷺ, for every messenger spoke in the language of his people.

There is a difference between the people of the call (qawm al-da'wah), who are the nation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the people of reception (qawm al-istiqbal), who are the nations before the nation of Muhammad ﷺ.

The earlier nations were not required to convey the call of the messengers who were sent among them. As for the nation of Muhammad ﷺ, it is required to do so, because Allah, glorified is He, sent His Messenger ﷺ, and He informed us in the Qur'an that among His signs is that He made people of different tongues (alsina mukhtalifah).(1)

It would not have been reasonable for Him to send a messenger who speaks all languages, so he ﷺ descended among the Arab nation. When they received him and the love of faith was imbued (ushribat)(2) into their hearts, it became incumbent upon them to spread out with the call, to convey the meaning of the Qur'an as proof, after they had received it as a miracle.

The Qur'an is a proof because it governs the movement of life, and the movements of life do not differ among all people, just as every civilization takes the scientific achievements of another and translates them into its own tongue, the one it speaks.

The translation of meanings from one language into another is a matter known in all the civilizations of the world, because the matter in its essence is a matter of meanings, and meanings do not differ from one nation to another.

The Qur'an is meanings and a methodology suitable for all mankind, and it descended in Arabic because the gift of the Arab nation is excellence in language and speech. Thus that nation was given the task of receiving the methodology of God as a rhetorical miracle, and of sending it to the rest of the societies.

For this reason you can make a comparison between the lands that were opened by the sword and fighting, and the lands that were opened by peace and by the sight of a righteous Muslim exemplar. You will find that those who spread Islam in many corners of the earth relied on the righteous example.

You will find that they conveyed the religion through praiseworthy qualities and by applying the religion's methodology in their dealings with others, and for this reason people turned in large numbers to the religion of Allah.

Thus we find that the methodology of Islam carried a miracle of meanings, alongside being a miracle in the language in which it descended, which is the language of the Arabs.

And we find peoples who cannot read a single Arabic letter except in the mushaf, because they learned reading from the mushaf, and they relied on understanding the meanings in it through the translations made by Muslims who loved the Qur'an and transmitted it into other languages.

For this reason we find the saying of Allah, glorified is He:

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ (al-Qamar).

Thus we know that Allah, glorified is He, made the Mother of the Qur'an easy in the tongue of the Arabs first, then made it easy by making that nation to which the Qur'an was sent a nation that spreads its message, glorified is He. That is because messages desire conveyance, and the primary means of conveyance is speech, and its second means on the receiving side is the ear. So there must be speech first, then there must be an ear that knows the connotations of words, so that it hears this speech and applies it in behavior.

Just as we know that whoever hears the speaker must be aware and knowledgeable of the meanings of words, for what the ear hears, the tongue relates.

We have learned that language is the daughter of hearing, and every individual only speaks the language he heard in his environment. If you trace the chain of learning all speech, you will find yourself before the original root from which mankind learned speech, and that is Adam, peace be upon him.

Allah, glorified is He, has said:

﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them.(3)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

We know that language began as tawqifi (divinely taught) when Allah taught it to Adam, then Adam spoke it and his environment heard it, and it became wad'i (conventional) after that, and languages differed from one society to another.

Here Allah, glorified is He, said:

﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people.﴾ (Ibrahim).

Thus the Most High explained the reason for the sending of every messenger with the language of his people. And there is a verse in which He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them, they would not have believed in it.﴾ (al-Shu'ara').

And He also said:

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained? Is it non-Arabic and Arab?" Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness,(4) and it is for them blindness."﴾ (Fussilat).

So there is one who receives the Qur'an as a guide to direction and purifies his soul from turbidity, and there is one who receives the Qur'an and for whom there is blindness, and upon whose hearing is a covering, and fear and discomfort, because he is a disbeliever.

The reason, as we know, is that the occurrence of an event from one who commands it requires an action and a counterpart to the action.

I have previously given an example of one who drinks tea and blows on it to cool it a little, and this same person, when he goes out on a winter morning, blows on his hands to warm them. Thus he blows once to cool something, and blows another time seeking warmth.

The matter is not in the act of blowing, but in the reception by the tea of the air coming out of your mouth. Tea is hotter than the body's temperature, so it cools by blowing, while in winter the hand is colder than the body, so it receives the blowing by raising its temperature to equal the body's temperature.

Thus you find that the Qur'an is one, but the believer hears it and rejoices in it, while the disbeliever hears it and is wearied and burdened by it.

And He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until when they leave your presence they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?"﴾ (Muhammad).

Thus we find one who receives the Qur'an but does not submit to its meanings, and we find one who listens to the Qur'an and his heart becomes humble and is moved to respond to what the Most High enjoins.

So: we have now learned that language began as tawqifi and ended as istilahi (conventional). We took from Allah what He taught Adam of names, and tongues changed from one group to another, and thus the languages of the messengers differed according to the peoples to whom they were sent.

Every messenger makes clear to the people the methodology of Allah. When he makes this methodology clear, some receive it with faith in what he brought and guidance, and others receive it with disbelief and misguidance.

Whoever Allah has guided, his heart yearns toward this methodology, expels from his heart any other belief, searches into what the Messenger brought, and fills his heart with the methodology in which he finds rest in understanding and tranquility.

This is the opposite of one whose heart is occupied by a contrary matter, which he insists upon, not from conviction but from inability to scrutinize, study, and aspire. He should have expelled the misguiding matter from his heart, and searched, compared, inferred, and reflected well, then admitted into his heart the more acceptable matter. But he does not do so, unlike one whom Allah has guided.

Let no one say, "Since Allah has led us astray, why does He punish us?" Rather let every person know that the will is directed to the capacity for faith, but he did not summon it into his heart.

The Most High says:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad).

And He says:

﴿And He does not lead astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ (al-Baqarah).

That is: defiant disobedience has proceeded from them, because they filled their hearts with false matters, so when matters of truth came, they found no entry.

And here, in the verse that is the subject of our reflections, He, glorified is He, says:

﴿So Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He is the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ (Ibrahim).

So whoever turns toward misguidance, Allah increases him in misguidance, and his faith adds nothing to the dominion of Allah. Whoever believes secures for himself the safety of life and of what follows death; he is in life an element of good, and after death he finds life with the bounties of the Bestower, glorified is He, the Mighty who is not overcome, and the Wise who has decreed for every matter what He wills.

1 Allah, Most High, says: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your tongues and your colours.﴾ (al-Rum).
2 He imbued his heart with love of this; that is, it took the place of the drink. From it is the saying of Allah, Most High: ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts.﴾ (al-Baqarah), meaning the love of the calf. And "ushriba fi qalbihi hubbahu" means it mixed with him. [Lisan al-Arab, root sh-r-b].
3 Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them.﴾ (al-Baqarah): these are the names by which people know one another: human, animal, earth, sea, plain, mountain, donkey, and similar things among the nations and others. [Mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1/121].
4 al-Waqr: heaviness in hearing or deafness. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/35].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 5:

Then Allah, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs: "Bring your people out from the darknesses into the light, and remind them of the days of Allah. Indeed, in that are signs for every patient one, grateful."﴾

The signs that Allah sent with Moses, peace be upon him, and the miracles that occurred with him, which He explained and manifested to his people, are many. Our Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came with only one miracle, which is the Qur'an. As for the rest of the sensory miracles that occurred with the Messenger of Allah, they came to strengthen the hearts of the believers in his message, and no trace of them remains after that except the beneficial remembrance with which the righteous servants of Allah find comfort.

The abundance of the miracles that came with Moses, peace be upon him, shows that the people to whom he was sent were a people of clamour (lajaj) and dispute.(1) When the scholars counted the miracles that came with Moses, some of them found them to be nine signs, others found them to be thirteen miracles, and a third group found them to be fourteen.

To verify the identity of those signs, we must distinguish between the signs that were directed at Pharaoh and the signs that came for the Children of Israel. The staff that turned into a moving serpent and the hand that shines are for Pharaoh. The Qur'an counted the signs that came with Moses for Pharaoh as nine signs. Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿Among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people.. 12﴾ (Al-Naml).

Moses was not asking Pharaoh to believe, for he was not sent to guide him. Rather, he came to silence him and to take the Children of Israel, to whom he was sent. The signs are: the staff, placing the hand into the pocket so that it comes out white, the loss of lives and fruits, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. These are the nine signs specific to Pharaoh.

As for the rest of the signs that Moses, peace be upon him, brought to the Children of Israel, they are many, such as:

﴿And when We raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy.. 171﴾ (Al-A'raf).

And also:

﴿And We shaded you with the clouds.. 57﴾ (Al-Baqarah).

And likewise the words of Allah, the Truth:

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails.. 57﴾ (Al-Baqarah).

Therefore Allah, glorified is He, summarised the signs that came with Moses for his people:

﴿And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs, [saying], "Bring your people out from the darknesses into the light, and remind them of the days of Allah.. 5﴾ (Ibrahim).

That is: restore to the focus of their awareness what was in the background, and let them recall from memory the days of Allah. What is meant is what happened on those days, just as we say "the Day of Badr," or "the Day of Dhi Qar," or "the Sixth of October," or "the Tenth of Ramadan."

In this noble verse, the reminder may be of those specific days, the events that happened to the peoples before them, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud, since Allah, glorified is He, had informed them of the stories of the earlier peoples and what each people did toward the messenger sent to them by Allah.

Or the reminder may be of the days on which Allah bestowed His blessings upon the Children of Israel, or tested them with what caused them pain, since Allah, glorified is He, said:

﴿And remind them of the days of Allah. Indeed, in that are signs for every patient one, grateful.. 5﴾ (Ibrahim).

The sabbar (patient one) is the one who greatly endures events with patience. It is a word that suggests that painful events occurred and need to be endured. Likewise, the word "shakur" (grateful) suggests blessed events that deserve gratitude.

Thus we find that the believer needs two things: patience with what causes pain, and gratitude for what is pleasing. When these two qualities come together in a believer, he is complete in faith.(7)

Allah, glorified is He, has said that these signs are evidences that clarify the path before the believer and give him a lesson, because when he knows the history of the earlier peoples, and finds that those among them who believed suffered some painful events but then received the good pleasure and blessings of Allah, and that those among them who disbelieved enjoyed a little, then were seized by the vengeance and wrath of Allah.

Here the believer advances to bear the hardships of faith, because he trusts that Allah, glorified is He, does not waste the reward of a believer, and the procession of faith must triumph. Therefore the believer is patient in trials and grateful for blessings.

(1) Al-lujjah and al-lajlajah: the mingling of voices. Al-lujjah: al-jalabah (uproar). And alajja al-qawm: when the people shouted. [Lisan al-Arab, root l-j-j].
(2) What is meant by "the people" here is the people of Pharaoh.
(3) Nataqa: he raised it from its place, shook it, and pulled it. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/252].
(4) Al-man: a dew resembling honey, which Allah sent down upon the trees as good food for the Children of Israel, but they denied Allah's favour upon them in that. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/240].
(5) Al-salwa: the quail (al-sammani), a small bird of the gallinaceous order, plump in body. It is one of the migratory birds that travel from Europe in winter to warm lands such as Egypt and Sudan, and what survives of them returns in early summer to its homeland in Europe. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/326].
(6) Ayyam Allah: the blessings of Allah. Also: the events of Allah among the earlier nations. Al-Tabari said: He admonished them with what had passed in the past days, that is, with what occurred in the days of Allah of blessing and trial, for they had been enslaved and humiliated. He mentioned the days alone because they were known to them. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 5/3678].
(7) On the authority of Suhayb al-Rumi, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "How wondrous is the affair of the believer! All of his affairs are good, and this is not so for anyone except the believer. If he is touched by something pleasing, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if he is touched by something harmful, he is patient, and that is good for him." Related by Muslim in his Sahih (2999).

The Most High then says:

﴿And [remember] when Moses said to his people: "Remember the favour of God upon you when He delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord."﴾

Thus we find the Most High presenting a model of the days of their suffering under the tyranny of Pharaoh, and how He delivered them from this tyranny. Pharaoh would impose upon them the harshest forms of torment, and "sāma" (سام) means he demanded it, so "sāma sū' al-'adhāb" (سام سوء العذاب) means he demanded the evil torment.

Pharaoh slaughtered their male children but did not slaughter the females, so that the women would be left without a provider and he could take them for himself, and in this there is severe humiliation.

Some orientalists paused at this verse and said: The Qur'an has already addressed this verse in Surat al-Baqarah, when He said:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ (Al-Baqarah)

So is this verse in Surat Ibrahim the more eloquent, or the verse in Surat al-Baqarah, especially since the difference between them is the coming of the "wa" (و) as a conjunction before the slaughter of the sons and the keeping alive of the women?

This orientalist added: And I will set aside what came in Surat al-A'raf when the Qur'an said:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment, slaying your sons and keeping your women alive. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ (Al-A'raf)

Naturally, this orientalist did not grasp the Qur'an through Arab linguistic competence, for if he had possessed this capacity of understanding, he would have known that the speech in these verses did not come from a single source, but from two sources.

In the verse of Surat al-Baqarah the speaking source is God, the Most High, and therefore He said: "We delivered you…" (Al-Baqarah).

But the speaking source in Surat Ibrahim is Moses, peace be upon him. He did not say that he himself delivered them, but rather enumerates the blessings with which God favoured them and reminds them of them, and the reason for this is that the great, when bestowing favours upon others, bestows only great things, whereas one who is less than great may bestow lesser things.

I cite this example for further clarification, not as a comparison, for He is far above comparison. Suppose a wealthy man has a poor brother, and the wealthy man may provide his poor brother with many things, and may take care of his children, looking after them and their upbringing completely. Then the poor man's son comes to the wealthy man's son and says: "Why do you not ask after us?" The wealthy man's son says: "Did not my father bring you this pen and that suit, in addition to the apartment you live in?"

But the wealthy uncle is content to say: "I do ask after you, as proof I have brought you the apartment you live in." So the truly great one is the one who mentions great matters, while the lesser is the one who enumerates things.

Here the Most High describes the scourge of torment and the slaughter of sons as a tremendous trial, in His saying: ﴿And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ (Ibrahim).

Thus we see the manifestation of the good with which God favoured them, namely deliverance from the slaughter of sons and the keeping alive of women for dishonour, and that was a kind of manifestation of evil. And this is a difficult trial.

We have previously explained that trial may be through good or through evil, for He said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.﴾ (Al-Anbiya').

So good is not a proof of honour, nor is evil a proof of humiliation, for He says:

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by giving him honour and blessing, he says: "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says: "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ (Al-Fajr)

Trial in its origin is examination: either you succeed in it or you fail, and therefore it is not blameworthy except by the outcome to which it leads.

1 Sāmahu al-amr yasūmuhu sawman: he imposed it upon him against his will. Al-Zajjaj said: it is most often used for torment, evil and oppression. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: s-w-m].
2 Istahyāhu: he kept him alive and did not kill him. God, the Most High, said: ﴿slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive﴾ (Al-Baqarah). That is: they slay the males only and leave the girls and women alive. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/183].
3 Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari said in his book (Fath al-Rahman bi-Kashf ma Yaltabis fi al-Qur'an), p. 27: ("If you say: What is the wisdom in omitting the conjunction here, and mentioning it in Surat Ibrahim? I say: Because what is here is the speech of God, the Most High, so it came as an explanation of what preceded it; and what is there is the speech of Moses, who was commanded to enumerate the trials in His saying: ﴿And remind them of the days of God﴾ (Ibrahim). So he enumerated the trials upon them, and so the mention of the conjunction was fitting.")

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 7:

He, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe."﴾

We note that the verse begins with the word (تأذّن, ta'adhdhana, "proclaimed"), and the whole root, alif, dhal, nun, is derived from the ear (adhn). The ear (udhn) is the instrument of hearing, the adhan (call to prayer) is an announcement, and "adhanahum" means he informed them.

And "ta'adhdhana" means: he made known with emphasis. Thus the meaning of the verse is: I inform you, with emphatic assurance from your Lord, that if you give thanks, He will surely increase you from His bounty and His giving, because thanks is evidence of a bond with the Giver, and that you have stripped yourselves of pride in what you have been given, and have known that He alone is the Bestower.

And the Truth, glorified is He, is the One who said:

﴿Nay! Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ (al-'Alaq)

Had man been bound to the Truth, glorified is He, the Truth would not have been separated from His blessings, and he would have remained mindful of the One who bestowed the blessings upon him.

For this reason I always say: beware lest blessing preoccupy you from the Bestower, for the blessing is given to you, and is not inherent in you.

The contrast comes directly after that, so He says:

﴿And if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe.﴾ (Ibrahim)

Here a question arises: does the one who does not thank God for His blessings become a disbeliever (kafir)?

Here we must know that there is a difference between kufr (disbelief) and kufran (ingratitude), but the word kufr came here to intensify the meaning of not giving thanks, and He did not use the word kufran, and He said:

﴿And if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe.﴾ (Ibrahim)

The parallel for this is the Truth's saying, glorified is He:

﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people who are able to find thereto a way. And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free from need of the worlds.﴾ (Al 'Imran, 97)

Whoever does not perform the pilgrimage is disobedient, as if God wishes to make neglecting the pilgrimage gravely serious. Or: the verse intends two rulings: the first ruling: belief in the obligation of pilgrimage, and the second: actually performing the pilgrimage.

For the Truth, glorified is He, has said:

﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people who are able to find thereto a way.. ﴾ (Al 'Imran, 97)

So whoever believes that this is a valid and binding ruling and believes in it, but does not carry it out, may fall into sin, because he is able to perform pilgrimage and did not do so.

As for one who disbelieves in pilgrimage itself and denies the whole matter, he is a disbeliever, and we seek refuge in God.

Here the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe."﴾ (Ibrahim)

Thus disbelief came in contrast to gratitude, and there must be punishment for disbelief, and God's punishment must be severe, because punishment is proportionate to the power of the one who punishes, and none is more powerful than God. We seek refuge in Him, glorified is He, from His punishment, for it is something that cannot be endured.

1 Kufr here means denial of blessing, which is the opposite of gratitude, and a kafir man is one who denies God's blessings. And one says: kafara ni'mat Allah, bi-ni'mat Allah, kufran and kufuran (he denied the blessing of God). [Lisan al-'Arab, root k-f-r]..

Allah, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾

Moses said this so that no one among his people would suppose that Allah has need of their thankfulness, or that He would punish them with torment if they disbelieved in His gratitude. So he wished to remove this assumption from the minds of those who heard him.

He made clear to them that the Truth, glorified is He, will not increase in anything by your faith, and that this faith from them and from all the people of the earth together will add nothing to His dominion, because the dominion of Allah is manifested by Him with the attributes of perfection, and it arises from a perfection that already exists.

And for this reason comes His saying, the Truth:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, and 'Ad...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 14, verse 9:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them but Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands to their mouths and said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with, and we are truly in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾

This noble verse gives us an explanation of His, glory be to Him, saying:

﴿And there was no community but that a warner had passed among them.﴾ (Fatir).

And likewise His saying:

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those whom We have related to you, and among them are those whom We have not related to you...﴾ (Ghafir).

We know that the Truthful, glory be to Him, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should inform his people about some of the prophets who preceded him. This is clear in His saying:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Thamud...﴾ (Ibrahim).

He says, glory be to Him, about the peoples who came after that:

﴿And those after them, none knows them but Allah. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs...﴾ (Ibrahim).

That is: the messengers carried the method of Allah, and likewise the miracles indicating their truthfulness for those who came after that. The "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) may be the miracles that indicate their truthfulness; or they are the verses containing clear rulings that organize the course of their lives so as to make them happy.

But did those peoples accept those clear proofs?

No, because the Truthful, glory be to Him, says of them:

﴿So they put their hands to their mouths and said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with..."﴾ (Ibrahim).

Thus we see that the disbelievers are those who put their hands to their mouths. Or they bit their hands with their back teeth, because they could not bear to apply the method of Allah and could not control themselves.

Or: they returned their hands to their mouths, meaning they said to the messengers, "Hiss!" (i.e., be silent and do not speak the message you have brought). Or: some of them said to the messengers, "There is no benefit in your speech to these people."

The richness of the Qur'an bears all these meanings, and the verse accommodates all of them. A single expression in the Qur'an includes bounties that suit the perfections of Allah, and the perfections of the Qur'an will remain; some of them appear to us, and we may not perceive others until Allah informs us of them on the Day of Resurrection.

Their saying:

﴿"We disbelieve in what you have been sent with..."﴾ (Ibrahim).

comes to reveal to us their foolishness, for they acknowledge that these are messengers from heaven, while at the same time they deny the method and openly declare this denial. This is revealed by His, exalted be He, saying:

﴿"And we are truly in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾ (Ibrahim).

That is: they declared their opinion about the method, and said that they are bewildered and doubt this method.

Note 1. Khala: passed and preceded. And "the bygone generations" (al-qurun al-khaliya) are those that have gone by. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: kh-l-w]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 14, verse 10:

The Qur'an presents the rejection of the messengers in the words of the True One, glory be to Him:

﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God, Originator (fatir) of the heavens and the earth? He calls you so that He may forgive you some of your sins and defer you to a specified term." They said: "You are only human beings like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾

His saying: ﴿Is there doubt about God…﴾ (Ibrahim) is a kind of address that does not leave the one addressed to answer except as you wish.

You do not do this except when you are confident that the one you address will answer, if he brings the truth to mind, as you wish.

For this reason the address here did not come with the words "There is no doubt about God," which would make the statement declarative. Someone might say: this is a false statement. But although the listeners are unbelievers, the speaker presents the matter in the form of a question, entrusting them that they will turn the matter over in their minds and will find the answer which they cannot deny, namely "There is no doubt about God."

Thus we find that the speaker has passed over their declaration of disbelief at first, and brought them a question which they will answer with "There is no doubt about God," and brings them the proof which admits of no doubt, which is His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (Ibrahim).

The fatir (Originator) is the One who creates a creation without a prior model (1), like the saying of the True One:

﴿Originator (badi') of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (al-Baqarah, 117) (2).

No one is able to create the like of the heavens and the earth, which were created without a prior model. And He, glory be to Him, is the One who willed that man should be master of all created beings, and that those beings should be subjected to his service.

Man may imagine that his own creation is greater than the creation of the heavens and the earth, so the True One, glory be to Him, admonishes him:

﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind…﴾ (Ghafir, 57).

If you look at the sun and ask yourself: how many generations have enjoyed its warmth and benefited from it? Surely you will not know the number of generations, because the sun was created before the creation of mankind, and every person enjoys the sun and benefits from it for the number of years of his life, then goes to death.

We find the great exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (3) setting forth the example which no one can deny, which indicates the innate nature (fitrah) of faith, and makes clear that the True One did not leave man to wait until his intellect matured in order to feel the necessity of faith. He gives the example of a small child who sneaks in and strikes his brother. Here the brother must turn to discover who struck him, because man from the beginning knows that nothing happens without a doer.

Suppose a child came and found his brother sitting on a chair, and he wanted to sit on the same chair. Here the child would pull and drag his brother off the chair so that he himself might sit, as if he had discovered by nature that two cannot be contained by one place.

Thus man reaches by nature the knowledge that there is one unique Creator.

So we find the saying of the True One:

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (Ibrahim)

is the broad cosmic sign.

After that He says:

﴿He calls you so that He may forgive you your sins…﴾ (Ibrahim).

This saying indicates mercy, wisdom, power and tenderness; and here He says:

﴿so that He may forgive you some of your sins…﴾ (Ibrahim).

He did not say "forgive you your sins," because He is addressing the unbelievers, whereas when He addresses the believers He says:

﴿O you who believe, shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment? That you believe in God and His Messenger, and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your lives; that is better for you, if you only knew. He will forgive you your sins…﴾ (al-Saff).

Thus the True One does not equate, in His address, between believers and unbelievers.

Or: what is meant by His saying ﴿so that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾ (Ibrahim) is the forgiveness of major sins, since minor sins are forgiven by performing the obligatory duties and acts of worship. We know that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The five prayers, and the Friday prayer to the next Friday, are expiation for what is between them, so long as major sins are not committed." (4)

Then He continues:

﴿and defer you to a specified term…﴾ (Ibrahim).

We all know that the term (ajal) is the fixed time appointed for an event. If the True One, glory be to Him, willed destruction, we find what indicates it in the saying of the True One:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling…﴾ (al-Qasas, 81) (5),

as He did with Qarun.

Or: His saying ﴿to a specified term﴾ (Ibrahim) is meant to refer to the Day of Resurrection.

But the unbelievers are people of contention and obstinacy, so we find their saying:

﴿They said: "You are only human beings like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾ (Ibrahim).

Thus it is declared that the unbelievers' answer to their messengers is that they prefer to be people who follow the traditions of their fathers. Had they reflected, they would have known that if imitation spread through societies, no one would have advanced beyond his fathers and forefathers, for the world develops through the rebellion of one generation against the previous one. Why then do these unbelievers insist on keeping the imitation of fathers and grandfathers?

And if the sons develop in everything, why do these unbelievers keep the fathers' imitation in beliefs?

Nor do the people of disbelief content themselves with this; they demand that the messengers bring them a clear authority (sultan mubin). Sultan is used once for compulsion upon an act, where the doer compelled is averse to the act; and once for a proof that persuades to the act, where the doer loves what he undertakes. Religion cannot spread by compulsion; rather a person must turn to religion with his heart, and that does not come by force.

For this reason we find the True One's saying:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion. Right guidance has become distinct from error…﴾ (al-Baqarah, 256).

Since right guidance has become manifest, there is no room for compulsion, for one who is compelled to something cannot truly adopt what he is compelled to.

And if a person enters religion, he must abide by what religion obliges him to; therefore a person cannot enter religion under compulsion, but must enter it with insight.

He is of Qurashi lineage, originally from Tabaristan. He is called (Ibn al-Khatib al-Ray). He travelled to Khwarazm, Transoxiana and Khurasan, and died in Herat in the year 606 AH. [al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 6/313]..
